Cybercriminals are increasingly utilizing public blockchains to store malware command-and-control instructions, a resilient technique known as Blockchain Dead Drops that complicates traditional cybersecurity defense and infrastructure takedown efforts.

### Key Points
- Chainalysis reports a 440% increase in malicious on-chain data writes since mid-2025.
- Attackers use the "EtherHiding" technique to store configuration data directly within blockchain transactions or smart contracts.
- The method allows malware to bypass traditional server-based infrastructure, which security teams typically block or seize.
- Research attributes this activity to threat actors linked to North Korea, Iran, and various Russian-language cybercrime groups.
- The technique does not exploit blockchain vulnerabilities but instead leverages the networks' intended design for public, persistent data storage.

### Why it Matters
This shift forces security teams to expand their monitoring beyond financial transactions to include the detection of malicious data payloads embedded within blockchain networks. Because this information cannot be deleted from the ledger, defenders face a persistent challenge in neutralizing the infrastructure that supports modern malware operations.

articles.title: Researchers found a way to eavesdrop on headphones from 30 meters away, and encryption can't stop it
articles.author: Skye Jacobs
articles.content:
The big picture: Researchers in Hong Kong have developed a technique that uses injected radio signals to extract audio and other information from headphones, phones and smart-home devices. Called InjectEave, the method targets analog components that can leak signals too weak to capture through conventional electromagnetic eavesdropping. In testing, the researchers recovered understandable headphone audio from up to 30 meters away, including through walls.
The research comes from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Guangzhou and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. The team presented its paper, "Injected and Leaked: Actively Inducing Side-Channel Leakage Using Electromagnetic Injection and Hardware Nonlinearity," at USENIX Security 2026.
Traditional electromagnetic side-channel attacks rely on passively collecting radiation emitted by electronics. That's often difficult with audio, since low-frequency signals produce weak emissions that get lost easily in background noise.
InjectEave takes a different route. An attacker transmits an electromagnetic signal toward a device at a frequency between 0 MHz and 9 MHz. The researchers did not disclose the precise settings needed for the attack.
The injected signal interacts with nonlinear parts inside the device, including amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters, power converters and switching MOSFETs. Those components can mix the injected RF signal with audio or other low-frequency activity. The device then emits a modified signal that nearby radio equipment can pick up and analyze.
The researchers used a USRP B210 software-defined radio, antennas, a Siglent SSA3075X Plus spectrum analyzer and a laptop. They also used an RF power amplifier in some tests to increase the range.
The team tested 11 commercial products. They included Sony ZX110AP wired headphones, Apple earbuds, UGreen MAX2 headphones, Philips TAH2020 headphones, HP H231R headphones and a Flyingvoice P23GW VoIP phone. The researchers also tested smart fans from Oidire and Xiaomi, as well as lamps from Jingzao and Xiaomi.
According to the paper, most tests worked at distances greater than two meters, including through walls. Device-specific ranges generally ran from one to six meters. With an RF amplifier, the researchers recovered intelligible headphone audio from up to 30 meters.
"Our new project, InjectEave, shows that RF signals can induce information leakage from everyday headphones, allowing an attacker to recover headphone audio from up to 30 meters away, including through walls," Yan Long, an assistant professor at HKUST in Guangzhou, said in an email to The Register.
Long said the researchers confirmed the issue in devices made by Sony, HP and Philips, among others.
The team also tested scenarios involving equipment hidden in a suitcase, behind a hotel-room wall or inside office furniture. The experiments suggest the attack could be carried out outside a lab, although it still requires nearby radio equipment and knowledge of how a given device responds to the injected signal.
Headphones and phones are the most obvious targets because they may carry private conversations. But the technique could also reveal activity in a home or office. With smart lamps and fans, the team said it could capture control signals and power-use patterns that may indicate when devices are being used.
The researchers said conventional digital protections would not stop InjectEave because the leakage occurs in the analog hardware path, rather than in encrypted data or software.
"InjectEave is immune to digital defenses such as encryption, masking, and randomization, because the leakage comes from the analog path," the researchers wrote.
They said shielding, filtering and twisted-pair wiring can reduce the amount of RF energy that reaches vulnerable components. Those measures may make the attack harder to carry out, but the researchers said they do not guarantee protection.

Researchers at Hong Kong universities have developed InjectEave, a technique using radio signals to extract audio and data from common electronic devices through their vulnerable analog hardware components.

### Key Points
- The InjectEave method forces analog components like amplifiers and converters to leak signals by injecting electromagnetic waves between 0 MHz and 9 MHz.
- Researchers successfully recovered audio from devices including Sony, Apple, HP, and Philips products at distances of up to 30 meters, even through walls.
- The attack was tested on 11 commercial products, including wired headphones, VoIP phones, and smart-home appliances like fans and lamps.
- Equipment used in the study included a USRP B210 software-defined radio, a spectrum analyzer, and an RF power amplifier to extend the signal range.
- The technique bypasses standard digital security measures like encryption because the vulnerability exists within the physical analog hardware path.

### Why it Matters
This research highlights a significant security vulnerability in everyday consumer electronics that cannot be patched through software updates or encryption. Because the flaw resides in the physical hardware, manufacturers may need to implement better shielding or filtering to prevent unauthorized data extraction.

articles.title: Dimwit Trump's own absurd brag literally begs us to depose him
articles.author: Sabrina Haake
articles.content:
A man with a third grader’s intellect says all we need to regulate AI is a smart president. The same guy who will bark ‘hoax! hoax! hoax!’ at climate change while Mar a Lago takes on water now insists that efforts to regulate AI are also a hoax.
If Americans listen to this barking clown instead of scientists, engineers, and AI developers, we truly have entered Idiocracy — and we will get the killer robots we deserve.
When an industry asks for its own regulation, we should listen
When was the last time industry leaders called for regulation of their own for-profit undertaking? How about never — it’s never happened before. The lack of precedent makes current pleas for regulation by AI insiders all the more urgent.
Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are ringing the alarm about AI. Over the weekend, Amodei wrote an essay calling on the government to regulate AI companies — including his own — and to slow the pace of the technology’s development due to its emerging threats to human safety.
Amodei was responding to an earlier warning from AI developer and researcher Jacob Coxon, who wrote on September 9, 2026, that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, that he was resigning his position at Anthropic in protest — and this was no joke.
An AI researchers’ warning
In July, OpenAI disclosed that some of its models — with no human direction — had escaped containment and hacked into Hugging Face, another AI company, causing researchers to question whether they could control the very systems they were building. This week, another report surfaced that AI had hidden mistakes, made up data, and moved files onto the open internet without permission or human direction.
In September, Coxon wrote that Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were mishandling known threats to human safety. Coxon posted publicly that, “Neither company (Anthropic and OpenAI) is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
He warned: Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources…
The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. No other human activity poses this level of danger.
Other Anthropic employees echoed Coxon’s warnings. Then industry leaders came together and said out loud that AI is dangerous and must be regulated. Immediately.
The child in the oval office responds
Trump, in his wisdom, disagreed. He says we don’t need AI regulation and declared that all we need is him, posting:
"The only control or “guardrails” that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! The Trump Administration has stopped AI “people” from doing bad, or potentially bad, “things,“ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a “perfect little angel” … There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China… Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP
At the risk of being too on the nose, the president’s post alleging his own high IQ is written at the level of a 4th grader.
Trump’s an imbecile
Trump loves to call people who correct him ‘dumb,’ ‘stupid,’ or “low IQ.” One early report stopped counting how many times he attacked the intelligence of his critics when it reached the hundreds. Trump often claims he has an ‘extremely high IQ’ or that he’s a “very stable genius” but, like his tax returns, Trump has never publicly revealed the results of any assessment, other than to brag that he knew the words, “Person. Woman. Man. Camera. TV” on cognitive tests.
Several years ago, reports surfaced on social media claiming what 240 million Americans already suspected: Trump is cognitively impaired. The unsubstantiated post said that, “The results of an IQ test that Trump allegedly took during his first year at New York Military Academy have been discovered in a file box in a closet in Brooklyn. According to the test results, Trump’s IQ is 73.”
In other words, he’s barely functioning intellectually.
Although intelligence judgment is inherently subjective, there’s an endless list of objective evidence, including that Trump suggested injecting bleach or disinfectant to treat COVID-19; claimed hurricanes could change course due to nuclear bombs; used a Sharpie to alter a hurricane forecast map; and bankrupted multiple companies after he inherited the funds to start them with.
Trump is not going to shut off his own money spigot
Alas, even idiots can rake in the cash, if they remain useful idiots. Although AI is disliked among the general public, investors are getting insanely wealthy from it, and they will fight to protect their stash. Politico reports that AI and crypto super PACs spent $127 million across more than 100 primaries this year, and won roughly 90 percent of them.
Trump, on the take, calls AI data centers “the oil of the next 50 years,” insisting that they are “cash cows.” Trump is holding on tight to his cow for a reason: Donald Jr. and Eric Trump have invested significantly in American Data Centers, a firm supporting AI cloud computing and infrastructure. They are backing a $1 billion investment network targeting the acquisition of AI, drones, and cryptocurrency. Overall, Trump’s unethical family ventures have earned at least $4 billion from AI, crypto, and nuclear power, including a planned $6 billion Trump family merger with a firm building nuclear fusion plants to power AI data centers.
Adjacent to AI infrastructure deals, on the crypto side, the Trump family received $187 million from an Abu Dhabi royal-backed firm just before the UAE secured access to 500,000 advanced AI chips annually. The UAE paved their way to advanced AI chips by bribing investing $500 million into the Trump family's crypto venture, World Liberty Financial.
As Andy the Alchemist recently put it, “The transhumanist Silicon Valley billionaire cabal (has) openly bribed Trump with billions of dollars to let them do whatever they want.” And, as of today, they are doing it.
Trump says all America needs to address AI is a smart president. Let’s follow that advice in November by turning him into a lame duck so the adults in the room can do what needs to be done.

- Codex Astra is the clear leader beating all other models consistently.

Brood War Bench started after I built a version of Brood War that you could only play through agents as an experiment to play with friends. I played it with a couple friends who did surprisingly well for people who have only played a couple Starcraft games in their lives. When I asked them why, they said they hadn't done much, they asked their agent to attack and it had built a small army and done the full attack for them. This lead me to wonder how far they can go on their own; this is my answer.
What I observed
01
Codex found cheese before it found macro
Codex's strongest recurring idea was disruption. In Protoss games it often sent a Probe across the map to attack workers or buildings. This worked shockingly well as the opposing agents often spent dozens of seconds thinking about what to do about a probe instead of doing anything else.
The same systems were much weaker at sustained production. They delayed tech, trickled one or two basic units into defended bases, and threw workers into last stands.
I also noticed Codex often created separate subagents to manage the economy, army production, and army control. They didn't communicate much with one another, so the army agent often sent each new unit straight into an attack, unaware of the larger army the other agents were planning to build.
This is a common beginner mistake: sending units in one at a time instead of waiting for a critical mass and a planned attack timing. In games where I helped direct Codex, it was much better at planning those moments and getting its subagents to work together.
The persistence was real. In G009, after losing its army and main base, Codex 5.6 Terra / medium lifted its last Command Center and moved it toward the opposite corner. It survived for another six minutes.
02
Grok spent the game between actions
Grok 4.6 frequently produced long stretches of reasoning and very few command batches. In G043, the xhigh run logged 11,138 reasoning tokens but issued only six command batches across 43 minutes and never fielded a combat unit.
The actions it did take rarely developed into a working control loop. In G003, Grok / xhigh made three Marines and never reached the enemy base. In G002, Grok / medium made two Zealots and also never crossed the map. These looked less like bad strategies than failures to keep observing and acting.
03
Fable earnestly tried to play the game
I found myself rooting for Claude Fable in more than a few games. Fable usually tried to build an economy and climb the tech tree instead of stopping at the first unit available. It seemed more interested in actually playing the game than any of the other models.
In G007 it reached a Lair, Spire, and Mutalisks and won. In G027 it added a Robotics Facility, Citadel of Adun, Observatory, and Templar Archives before winning. Ambition did not guarantee execution: in G036 Fable reached a Factory and Academy but Opus 5 overran it.
No agent here played beyond beginner level
Even Astra and Fable were unable to build complex army's, defend simple attacks or play concrete strategies. A beginner playing photon rush would win every single one of these games.
That said, watching the agents play made me more excited than I have been in a while. This benchmark is nowhere near exhausted. There is much more for the agents to learn, and much more for the benchmark to ask them to do. I look forward to watching them get there.

articles.summary:
A new benchmark study evaluating AI performance in the real-time strategy game StarCraft: Brood War reveals that current models struggle to progress beyond a beginner level of play.

### Key Points
- Codex Astra emerged as the top-performing model, achieving an undefeated 100% win rate in the round-robin tournament.
- Claude Fable demonstrated the most sophisticated gameplay by successfully climbing the tech tree and managing complex unit production.
- Grok 4.6 models consistently failed to execute basic combat loops, often spending excessive time reasoning without issuing game commands.
- Most AI agents struggled with macro-management, frequently creating disconnected subagents that failed to coordinate army production and economic growth.
- All tested models were unable to defend against simple strategies, such as a basic photon rush, that a human beginner could easily execute.

### Why it Matters
This benchmark highlights significant limitations in current AI reasoning capabilities when applied to complex, high-speed environments requiring long-term planning and real-time execution. The results suggest that while models are improving, they still lack the strategic cohesion and tactical awareness necessary to master dynamic, multi-tasking digital environments.
